g.text: What "streaming" means — and the two clocks underneath it
9 events · 3 of 6 minutes get a different answer per clock
what someone might mean when they say "we need streaming"
an answer within a deadline — a latency promise
the same promise, without naming the deadline
the job never ends, unlike a batch run
each record triggers work, versus a scheduled sweep
an execution engine for UNBOUNDED data — nothing more
Only the last row is a statement about the ENGINE. The other five are statements about the ANSWER.
A team can agree they want "streaming" and disagree about every one of them, which is why the first job is to split the word.
Step 1/4 — the word "streaming" means five different things
Five of these six describe a property someone wants from the ANSWER — how fast it comes, how often, how exact. Only the last describes the SYSTEM.
Mixing the two is why "do we need streaming?" is a question two engineers can answer differently while agreeing on every fact.
What "streaming" means — and the two clocks underneath it
9 events · 3 of 6 minutes get a different answer per clock
THE BOOK'S NINE EVENTS — IN THE ORDER THE PIPELINE SEES THEM
event time = when it happened · processing time = when the pipeline saw it
The highlighted row is event 7: it HAPPENED at 12:00:50 and was SEEN at 12:04:40 — 230s apart.
Nothing is broken. A phone was offline, a queue backed up, a retry fired. This gap is the normal case, not the exception.
Step 2/4 — every event carries TWO timestamps, and they disagree
Read the two times on any row and they differ. Read event 7 and they differ by 230s — it happened in the first minute and arrived in the fifth.
Every difficulty in this book follows from that one gap, so the dataset is built to contain it rather than to be tidy.
What "streaming" means — and the two clocks underneath it
9 events · 3 of 6 minutes get a different answer per clock
THE SAME NINE EVENTS, COUNTED TWO WAYS
per-minute sum of v, by EVENT time (what users did) and by PROCESSING time (when we noticed)
3 of the 6 minutes get a DIFFERENT answer depending on which clock you count by.
No event was lost and no arithmetic is wrong. The two columns are counting two different questions.
Step 3/4 — count by the wrong clock and the answer changes
This is the whole problem in one table. Bucketing by processing time says the 12:00 minute saw 8; bucketing by event time says 12. 3 of 6 minutes
disagree. A processing-time dashboard is not a slightly-stale event-time dashboard — it answers a different question and can be arbitrarily far
What "streaming" means — and the two clocks underneath it
9 events · 3 of 6 minutes get a different answer per clock
the four questions, which are the next chapter and the rest of the book
the transformation — a sum, a count, a join
the windowing — which slice each value covers
the triggers and watermarks — a PROCESSING-time choice
the accumulation — does a new answer replace or add to the old
Only the third question is about processing time. The other three are about event time or about bookkeeping.
That split is why the table above was possible: WHERE is an event-time decision, WHEN is a processing-time one, and confusing them is the
Step 4/4 — so the book asks four questions of every pipeline
These four are not a summary — they are the book's actual structure, and the reason the previous step's table has two columns. WHERE picks the
event-time slice; WHEN picks the processing-time moment to speak. A system that only has "when" is a processing-time dashboard, which is the thing
